title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, Benchmarks & Runbooks
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime reference material used by the Eng - Serving Runtime team: runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design and policies, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, known issues, release notes summary, and operational runbooks. It is intended to be the canonical team wiki for on-call, performance investigations, and release planning.

Sections in this page:
1) Architecture overview
2) Kernel scheduling design and policies
3) Profiling playbook (how-to)
4) Benchmarking suite and test matrix
5) Release notes (recent/high-impact items)
6) Known issues and workarounds
7) Runtime runbooks (incidents and recovery)
8) Team wiki pointers, ownership, and change process

---

1) Architecture overview

Short intro: The Serving Runtime is a GPU-optimized inference engine with an orchestration/control plane. It balances latency SLOs, throughput, and cost by combining: model loaders, kernel selector, scheduler, continuous batching engine, KV/prefix cache, and request-level routing. The following components are owned by the Eng - Serving Runtime team unless otherwise noted.

Key components:
- API gateway / front proxy (ingress) — validates requests, enforces quotas, annotates telemetry. (owned by Eng Platform)
- Router & policy engine — applies routing policies (latency-first, cost-first, region affinity) and selects model variant fallbacks.
- Request dispatcher / batcher — groups compatible requests into micro-batches, maintains queue priorities and burst slots.
- Scheduler/executor — maps batches to GPU workers, selects execution kernels, allocates CUDA streams and memory pools.
- KV cache — per-worker prefix and KV cache for decoder-state reuse and partial response caching.
- Model runtime (loader) — handles model artifacts, quantized kernels, and runtime compilation/caching of kernels.
- Telemetry & tracing — per-token metrics, GPU counters, latency histograms, and sample traces for traceback.

Runtime deployment patterns:
- Hosted (multi-tenant) — elastic pools with smart routing and burst capacity.
- Dedicated — reserved GPU pools with pinned model variants and stricter isolation.
- Private (VPC/on-prem) — customer-managed network plus our control plane integration.

SLOs and guardrails (typical):
- 95th percentile decoding latency (per 1k tokens): <= 120ms for small models, <= 350ms for medium models (configurable by profile)
- Tail latency alert threshold: p99 >= 2x baseline SLO for 5m window
- Throughput SLO: sustained tokens/sec per GPU within 10% of benchmarked baseline for committed configs

Owners and contacts:
- Component owners: scheduler (Samir Gupta), kernel/runtime (Miguel Torres), profiling/benchmarks (Rebecca Lin).

---

2) Kernel scheduling design and policies

Design goals:
- Prioritize latency-sensitive requests while preserving batch efficiency for throughput workloads.
- Avoid head-of-line blocking and reduce fragmentation of GPU resources.
- Support graceful preemption and quick rollback to safe configurations on anomaly detection.

Scheduling primitives and concepts:
- Priority queues: each worker maintains 3 logical priority queues (hot/interactive, normal, background).
- Time-slicing window: interactive requests can preempt ongoing background batches if preemption budget is available.
- Continuous batching: compatible requests are coalesced until max_batch_size or max_hold_ms reached.
- Kernel affinity: scheduler prefers kernels that match model architecture and sequence-length distribution (reduces kernel churn).
- Memory lanes: separate memory pools for active KV caches vs. transient activation buffers to reduce OOMs during bursty traffic.

Policy examples (config knobs):
- interactive_batching.max_hold_ms = 8  # milliseconds to wait for coalescing
- interactive_batching.max_batch_size = 8
- background_batching.max_hold_ms = 50
- background_preemption_budget = 0.15  # portion of GPU cycles allowed for preemption per second
- kernel_churn_penalty = 0.2  # soft penalty in scheduler score when switching kernel families

Preemption model and semantics:
1. Soft preemption: pause accepting new background batches, allow in-flight micro-batches to complete within grace_window_ms (default 25ms).
2. Hard preemption (rare): abort background batches and reclaim memory, used when OOM risk detected or urgent latency SLO breach. Hard preemption requires operator confirmation in Dedicated/private by default.

Scheduling algorithm (high level):
- Score each pending batch: score = priority_weight * latency_urgency - kernel_switch_cost - estimated_gpu_time_penalty.
- Pick highest score and attempt placement on least-loaded CUDA device that satisfies memory and kernel constraints.
- If placement fails for > placement_retry_threshold (3 attempts), escalate to fallback model variant or region routing.

---

3) Profiling playbook (how-to)

Purpose: Provide a repeatable process for diagnosing performance regressions, tail latency, memory growth, and kernel inefficiencies. The playbook is used by on-call, performance eng, and release owners.

Tools we use:
- internal_perf_collector (our agent that emits per-token timing and GPU metrics)
- nvprof / nsight (for low-level GPU kernel timings)
- NVIDIA Nsight Systems & Nsight Compute for flamegraphs and kernel timelines
- PyTorch/Triton profiler (for operator-level breakdowns)
- perf & BPF tools (for CPU-side sampling)
- Prometheus + Grafana for long-term metrics and dashboards
- flamegraph.svg generator for trace visualizations

Profiling workflow (step-by-step):
1) Reproduce: capture a failing/regressing request via trace-id. Collect representative input (prompt + sampling params).
2) Baseline comparison: run the same request against the last known-good model and configuration (use bench harness).
3) Collect telemetry: enable verbose tracing for a single worker and collect per-token timings, kernel names, CUDA stream counters, and memory snapshots. Use a single-worker isolation to avoid cross-noise.
4) Low-level capture: run Nsight Compute on the same workload to capture kernel-level metrics (shared memory, SM utilization, occupancy).
5) Analyze: compare operator-level breakdown vs. baseline; look for increased kernel execution time, kernel queueing, or memory thrash.
6) Hypothesize: common causes include changed quantization kernels, new operator fusion, suboptimal kernel selection, heavy KV cache miss rate, or host-to-device transfer increases.
7) Experiment: toggle kernel selection flags, try alternate quantized kernels, adjust batch sizes, and re-run profiling. Document each trial.
8) Rollout plan: if fix is validated, prepare canary with traffic split (5% -> 25% -> 100%) and monitor token-level metrics and p99 latency.

Quick commands (examples):
- Collect internal trace: ./tools/trace-collect --trace-id <id> --out ./traces/<id>.json
- Run bench harness single-shot: ./bench/run.py --model <model> --promptfile sample.json --tokens 128 --workers 1 --profile nsight

What to capture in each profiling session (minimum):
- Model name & version, quantization profile, kernel family used
- Batch size distribution and sequence-length histogram
- Per-token latency histogram (p50/p95/p99)
- GPU SM utilization and achieved occupancy
- Memory high-water-mark and allocator fragmentation stats
- Kernel timeline with timestamps and blocking events

---

4) Benchmarking suite and test matrix

Purpose: Provide deterministic regression checks and capacity baselines for each model variant and hardware class. The bench suite is invoked by CI for release gating and used by SRE to validate fleet capacity.

Benchmark categories:
- Latency microbench: single-request p95/p99 at fixed token length and sampling params
- Throughput (sustained): max tokens/s for multi-worker steady-state under typical prompt distribution
- Scalability: tokens/s per GPU when adding workers and increasing concurrency
- Burst behavior: recoverability & tail-latency after synthetic burst load
- Cost/efficiency: tokens/$ measured with batcher configs and kernel choices

Standard test matrix (examples):
- small-model-cpu (dev)
- small-model-gpu.gpuA100.q8_0
- medium-model-gpuA100.fp16
- large-model-gpuH100.q4_1

Metrics collected:
- p50/p95/p99 decode latency (ms per 1k tokens)
- tokens/sec (sustained)
- GPU utilization (SM%) and GPU memory usage (GB)
- Kernel churn rate (kernel switches per 1k requests)
- Cost-per-1M-tokens estimate

CI gating rules (example):
- New runtime changes must not increase p95 latency by > 10% on small/medium default profiles in bench CI.
- Kernel scheduler changes must show no regression on throughput by > 7% on dedicated bench configs.

Benchmark harness usage (CLI example):
- ./bench/run-suite --suite default --model <model> --hardware A100 --out results/<model>-<date>.json

Result artifacts and storage:
- All bench runs produce JSON artifacts plus flamegraph SVGs stored in s3://redwood-bench-results/<model>/<date>/
- CI fails if artifact p95 or tokens/sec violate configured thresholds.

---

5) Release notes (recent/high-impact items)

2026-11-29 release (runtime v1.14.0) highlights:
- Improved kernel selection policy to reduce kernel churn on multi-length workloads (avg p95 down 8% on medium models).
- New continuous-batching heuristics: adaptive max_hold_ms based on recent latency percentiles.
- KV cache memory isolation: separate allocator to reduce OOMs for high-concurrency customers.
- Bench additions: burst-recovery test and cost-per-token reporting.

Action items after release:
- Monitor p99 tail latency dashboards for 48 hours and verify no increase >10%.
- Run targeted benchmarks for top 10 customer models in Dedicated.

---

6) Known issues and workarounds

KR-1041: Occasional p99 spikes when kernel churn is high for multi-length prompts.
- Symptoms: p99 latency spikes correlated with kernel switch events.
- Workaround: pin model to single kernel family with model_runtime.flags kernel_affinity=prefer_stable. Reduced spikes observed in canary testing.

KR-1102: Memory fragmentation leading to OOM during large-batch background workloads.
- Symptoms: worker OOMs seen during high background batch concurrency; typical HWM just below memory but allocation fails for transient large request.
- Workaround: enable background_batching.max_hold_ms reduction to increase chances of smaller batches, or enable memory_lanes.enabled = true to isolate KV cache.

KR-1188: Nsight capture overhead distorts short-duration kernel timings for interactive workloads.
- Symptoms: profiling run shows longer-than-expected kernels compared to production traces.
- Workaround: use internal_perf_collector with per-token sampling and only run nsight in isolated single-worker mode.

If you observe a new pattern: create an issue in the runtime team board, tag with KR- (kernel runtime) and include a minimal repro. Prioritize incidents with customer impact or SLO violations.

---

7) Runtime runbooks (operational procedures)

Runbook A: High p99 tail latency (interactive requests)
1. Confirm: Check p99 > alert threshold for > 5 minutes on the primary dashboard. Note affected models and regions.
2. Isolate: Identify worker(s) with highest tail (use trace ids).
3. Quick mitigation: move traffic off affected worker via router-based draining (route away) or reduce interactive.max_hold_ms to 1-2ms to minimize batching-induced latency.
4. If kernel churn suspected: temporarily pin stable kernel family: model_runtime.flags kernel_affinity=prefer_stable for affected model variant.
5. Collect traces and run profiling playbook steps.
6. Escalate: If mitigation fails within 20 minutes, page kernel/runtime owner and SRE lead.

Runbook B: OOMs / memory pressure on worker
1. Confirm: look for OOM traces and memory HWM alerts.
2. Reduce load: divert new requests to other workers (router policy) and set worker to draining state.
3. Try soft recovery: restart worker process (safe restart), if still OOMing, clear caches (kv-cache flush) and restart.
4. If repeated: change memory allocator knobs (increase fragmentation_threshold or enable memory lanes) and schedule a controlled canary.
5. Post-incident: add model to heavy-memory test matrix and update bench cases.

Runbook C: Throughput degradation (sustained tokens/sec drop)
1. Check for background job interference (maintenance tasks), network saturation or hardware telemetry (PCIe errors).
2. Validate scheduler metrics: queue lengths, batch sizes, kernel_churn rate.
3. Scale up temporary capacity and run bench harness to compare expected tokens/sec.
4. If config regression suspected, quickly rollback the runtime config change via feature-flag pipeline.

Runbook D: Canary rollback process
1. Stop canary scale and freeze routing for the canary variant.
2. Switch 100% of canary traffic back to previous model variant/config in the router policy.
3. Perform post-rollback verification: run 50 synthetic requests and verify latency histograms match baseline.
4. Create postmortem and schedule follow-up remediation.

Where to find more granular pages:

Ownership & change process:
- Code owners: folder runtime/core (kernel selection), runtime/scheduler, runtime/batcher. All runtime PRs must include a bench run artifact and a profiling comparison (unless purely docs change).
- Release process: runtime changes go through feature flag canary (5% -> 25% -> 100%). Large kernel or allocator changes require a 72-hour extended canary with SRE monitoring enabled.
- Documentation updates: update this wiki and add a short note to the release notes for each runtime release.

Appendix: Recommended default config table
- interactive_batching.max_hold_ms: "8"
- interactive_batching.max_batch_size: "8"
- background_batching.max_hold_ms: "50"
- background_preemption_budget: "0.15"
- memory_lanes.enabled: "true"
- kernel_churn_penalty: "0.2"
